title: The golden lion
hook: Fazang explains Huayan to the empress with a golden lion, and a room of mirrors

segments.voice: Yesterday, Zhiyi, who sorted the sutras and gave everything its place. What did you sort, and what did you decide to keep? Day nine hundred eighty-five.

A sutra so vast that an imperial court can't get hold of it. So the empress of China, who rules in her own name, asks a monk to explain it. Tradition says the monk doesn't open a book. He points across the palace hall to a statue standing there, a lion made of gold, and begins to talk about it. On another day, tradition says, he lines a room with mirrors, facing one another on every side, and sets a lamp and an image of the Buddha in the middle. Then he invites her in. Today, Fazang.
screen: `AN EMPRESS ASKS A MONK.` → `A LION MADE OF GOLD.` → `A ROOM LINED WITH MIRRORS.`

segments.voice: First, the teacher. The monk is Fazang, a master of the Huayan school, named for the Flower Garland Sutra, and the empress is Wu Zetian. Second, the lion. Fazang asks her to look at it two ways. There is the gold, which has no shape of its own, and there is the lion, the shape the gold has taken. Without gold there's no lion. Without some shape, the gold isn't anything you can see. In his essay on the golden lion, the gold stands for the deep nature of things, and the lion stands for the world of particular things. They are not two. And more: every part of the lion is gold, so each single hair of the lion, the essay says, holds the whole lion. Third, the mirrors. Stand in that room and the lamp appears in every mirror, and in every mirror's reflection of every other mirror, without end. Huayan teaches that the world is like this: each thing reflects every other, and holds them all inside it. The Flower Garland Sutra is linked with an image of the same idea, a net hung with jewels, each jewel shining with the light of all the rest. Fourth, why it matters on an ordinary day. In Huayan's picture, if every thing contains every other thing, then no one is a side character. The neighbor, the stranger on the stairs, the person you argued with: in this teaching, each one holds a reflection of the whole, and so does the one listening.
screen: `FAZANG, THE EMPRESS, AND HUAYAN.` · `THE GOLD AND THE LION ARE NOT TWO.` · `A LAMP IN EVERY MIRROR.` · `NO ONE IS A SIDE CHARACTER.` · then, large: `MIRRORS IN MIRRORS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look at a reflection in a reflection. If there's a window, a phone screen or a glass near you, look at how it holds the room, and how something in the room might hold it back. If not, close your eyes. Bring one person to mind, and then notice who is reflected in them: who raised them, who taught them, who fed them. Then notice yourself reflected there too. Let the reflections run on as far as they go, then rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Fazang. The Huayan master who showed the empress a golden lion to teach that the gold and its shape are not two, and that every part holds the whole. Today's word.

Your line: mirrors in mirrors. Today, with one person you'd usually pass without a thought, remember Fazang's mirrors: in his picture, that person holds the whole room too. Day nine hundred eighty-five.

howItsDone: In Huayan and related traditions in China, Korea and Japan, students study the Flower Garland Sutra and Fazang's Essay on the Golden Lion, and teachers still use images like Indra's net and facing mirrors to explain how all things interpenetrate.

fork.setup: an empress asks you to explain a vast sutra her court can't follow. you're Fazang. what do you do?
options: point to the golden lion in the hall
tell her it is too deep to explain
fork.reveal: Fazang used the golden statue: the gold and the lion's shape are not two, and every part holds the whole.

original.note: Chinese Huayan: flower garland, the name of the sutra and of Fazang's school.

trapdoor: what you thought: a nice parable about a gold statue.
what it means: the gold is the deep nature of things, the lion the world of particulars; they are not two, and every part holds the whole.

what a scholar hears: Huayan's interpenetration (each thing containing all things) worked out through two teaching devices, the Golden Lion essay and the mirror room, alongside the sutra's net of jewels.

notes: Editor: varied the hook opening; framed the golden-lion scene as tradition; 'every whisker' corrected to the essay's 'each hair holds the whole lion'; the closing now reports Huayan's view instead of the narrator asserting it; swapped the cashier and bus driver, which repeated day 970's practice.
The mirror room is framed as 'tradition says'; the number of mirrors (often given as ten) is left out under the claims rule.
Gold as principle (li) and lion as phenomena (shi): paraphrased from the Golden Lion essay; confirm the plain-English glosses.
'Every whisker holds the whole': paraphrases the essay's point that each hair contains the whole lion; confirm.
Indra's net is attributed to the Flower Garland Sutra 'linked with'; strictly the image is developed in Huayan commentary drawing on the sutra. Confirm the phrasing.
Wu Zetian described as 'an empress who rules in her own name'; confirm.
Audit: 'royal court' corrected to 'imperial court' for Empress Wu; the carry's 'they hold the whole room' was ambiguous (mirrors or people) and now names the person.
